newsitem.title: CANADA: GM Canada talks with union off for weekend.
newsitem.headline: GM Canada talks with union off for weekend.

text.p: Talks between General Motors Corp.'s Canadian unit and the union representing the automaker's 26,000 striking workers have been shelved for the weekend, making it certain the strike will push into its second week.
Canadian Auto Workers union President Buzz Hargrove said the bulk of the union's bargaining team went home on Thursday for the Canadian Thanksgiving long weekend.
"So this thing obviously is not going anywhere at least until sometime next week," Hargrove said after a brief meeting with GM Canada's lead negotiator, Dean Munger.
"We'll all come back here Tuesday morning and see where that takes us," said Hargrove.
Monday is a national holiday in Canada.
GM Canada spokesman Stew Low said Friday the GM negotiating team also decided to quit the talks for the weekend but that a "dialogue" will be maintained between the two leaders.
Munger and Hargrove have vowed to remain at the downtown Toronto hotel where the talks have taken place, but no developments were expected.
"Buzz and Dean will probably talk over the weekend," said Low. "It's all part of the process when you are so far apart to keep talking."

Bargaining has floundered since the escalating strike began Oct. 2. The key stumbling block remains GM's ability to shift work outside the company, usually to non-unionized suppliers, a practice known as outsourcing.
Hargrove continued to blame the stalled talks on GM Canada's parent company in Detroit.

"There has been a decision made by people that are a lot higher than people in this hotel to leave the bargaining on hold for a bit," said Hargrove. "I guess the only good news is they're not packing up their bags and leaving the hotel and saying, 'We'll call you in two or three weeks.'"

GM said the total number of U.S. workers affected by the CAW walkout remained relatively low, at 2,000. The carmaker has 950 workers idled at its Ypsilanti, Mich., plant and 1,050 idled at its North Tonawanda, N.Y., engine plant near Buffalo.
Neither side was willing to speculate how long the work stoppage would last, but both seem resigned for a long haul.
"I hope everyone is not waiting with bated breath for some new development," Hargrove told reporters at his daily news briefing on Thursday. "Are you getting as resigned as I am?"
GM's Low said Munger is "extremely tenacious" and willing to talk as long as it takes to reach a settlement.
"He's trying to find the right common ground to solve this issue and that's just going to take time," said Low.

Hargrove has said the union's $37 million strike fund could last at least 12 weeks and stretch to 16 weeks if new credit is arranged. The CAW also has set a special dues meeting for Oct. 18 to raise funds from all its 210,000 members.
